blocks.prompt: The Goose That Knows the Way
blocks.text: A baby goose is called a gosling. It hatches out of an egg covered in soft yellow down. Almost right away it can walk. On its very first day it can swim. The gosling stays close to its mom and dad. Both of them watch it. If something comes too near, a goose stretches out its long neck and hisses. Geese eat grass all day long. In fall, when the days get short, the geese fly away to find warmer water. They fly together in the shape of a V, and they honk the whole way.

blocks.prompt: Why Geese Fly in a V
blocks.text: Look up in fall and you might see a line of geese crossing the sky. They are not flying in a V by accident. Flying is hard work. A goose flaps all day, and its muscles burn a lot of fuel. When a goose flaps, it pushes air down under its wings to hold itself up. That air has to go somewhere. It rolls off the wingtips and curls upward again. A goose flying just behind and a little to the side can ride that rising air. It gets a small amount of lift for free, so it does not have to flap quite as hard. The goose at the very front gets no free lift at all. It has the hardest job in the flock. So the geese take turns. When the leader gets tired, it drops back into the line and another goose moves up to the point. The honking helps too. Geese call to each other the whole flight, so every bird can hear where the others are. A flock of geese is a team that keeps trading places.

blocks.prompt: The Man the Geese Thought Was Mom
blocks.text: In the 1930s, a scientist in Austria named Konrad Lorenz tried something odd. He took a clutch of greylag goose eggs and sat beside them until they hatched. The goslings opened their eyes, and the first large moving thing they saw was Lorenz. From that moment, they followed him. They followed him across the grass. They followed him into the water. They called out when he walked out of sight. To those goslings, Konrad Lorenz was mom. Lorenz called this imprinting. A gosling is not born knowing what its mother looks like. It is born with a rule instead. The rule is roughly this: whatever big thing moves nearby and makes noise in my first hours, stay with that thing and learn it well. In a nest, the rule works perfectly, because the only big noisy thing there is the mother goose. The gosling learns her shape and her voice, and it never has to learn them again. The window slams shut fast. After a day or two, a gosling will not imprint on anything new. That is a good bargain for a bird that has to walk and swim on its first day. A gosling cannot afford a week of working out who its family is. It has to know now, and being wrong is better than being slow, because in a real nest the rule is almost never wrong. Lorenz shared a Nobel Prize in 1973 for this work. The photographs of a serious man in a heavy coat leading a parade of goslings across a field are still famous.

blocks.prompt: The Bird That Flies Over the Himalayas
blocks.text: Every spring, a goose does something that should kill it. The bar-headed goose spends winter on the warm plains of India. Its breeding lakes lie in Mongolia and on the Tibetan Plateau. Between the two stands the Himalaya, the highest wall of rock on Earth. The goose does not go around it. It goes over. Air at that height is thin. Near the summit of Everest, each breath holds about a third as much oxygen as a breath at sea level. Human climbers spend weeks letting their bodies adjust, and most still carry bottled oxygen. The bar-headed goose arrives from near sea level in a day or two, and it is not resting on the way up. It is flapping, which is one of the most fuel-hungry things any animal can do. Its body is built for the job. Hemoglobin is the molecule in blood that picks up oxygen in the lungs and drops it off in the muscles. The bar-headed goose has a version that grabs oxygen more tightly than ours, so it can still load up where there is almost nothing to load. Its lungs are large for its size, and it breathes deep and fast without the dizziness that would drop a person. Its flight muscles are threaded with extra capillaries, so blood reaches the working fibers quickly, and those fibers are crowded with mitochondria, the parts of a cell that burn fuel using oxygen. Scientists once assumed these geese simply cruised at extreme altitude for hours. Then researchers fitted them with tracking loggers and found something smarter. The geese hug the ground. They climb hard through the passes and sink again the moment the terrain allows, staying as low as the mountains will let them, because thicker air is easier air and altitude is only paid for when it is unavoidable. Most of the climbing happens at night, when the air is cooler and denser and calmer. Tracked birds have been recorded above 7,000 meters, higher than any mountain outside Asia, on nothing but muscle and blood.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: A flying flock of geese is a skein
Two rival theories: saving energy, or staying in view
1970: engineers calculated a V could stretch a flock's range by about 70 percent
2001: pelicans in formation showed lower heart rates
2014: ibis loggers caught birds timing wingbeats to catch upwash
The bird at the point pays the most, so the point keeps changing

blocks.prompt: The V: A Problem the Flock Cannot Talk About
blocks.text: A skein of geese crossing an October sky is one of the most familiar sights in nature, and for most of the twentieth century nobody could prove why they do it. There were two good guesses. The first was aerodynamic. A flapping wing throws air downward to hold the bird up, and that air has to go somewhere. It spills off the wingtip and curls into a spinning trail called a vortex. Directly behind the bird, the air is still being pushed down, which is bad air to fly in. But just behind and off to one side, that same trail is rolling upward. A bird sitting in the upwash is, in effect, standing on a moving escalator. It needs less power to stay in the sky. In 1970, two engineers named Lissaman and Shollenberger ran the numbers and estimated that twenty-five birds in a well-formed V could fly roughly seventy percent farther than a single bird flying alone. On paper, the V was a machine for saving fuel. The second guess was social. Perhaps the V has little to do with air. Perhaps it is simply the easiest shape in which every bird can see every other bird, hold its spacing, follow the leader, and never collide. A staggered line is a good shape for looking, not only for lifting. The problem was evidence. You cannot ask a goose. Wild flocks fly high, fast, and nowhere near instruments, and for decades the argument stayed theoretical. The first crack came in 2001. Researchers in France trained great white pelicans to fly behind a microlight aircraft and fitted them with heart rate monitors. Birds flying in formation had measurably lower heart rates than birds flying alone, and they glided more between flaps. Something about the formation was cheaper. The decisive test came in 2014, and it used a different bird for a practical reason. A conservation team in Austria was hand-raising northern bald ibises and teaching them a lost migration route by leading them with a microlight. The birds were tame, the route was known, and each one could carry a logger recording its exact position many times a second alongside the beat of its own wings. The data was startling. The ibises did not merely trail behind one another. They placed themselves almost exactly where the theory predicted the upwash would be, and they timed their wingbeats to the bird in front, so their own wings rose as the helpful air arrived. When a bird did end up directly behind another, in the downwash, it flipped to the opposite timing, as though dodging the bad air. Nobody taught them any of this. Each bird was solving a problem in fluid dynamics in real time, with no instruments and no way to describe what it was doing. None of that proves the social explanation wrong. Both are probably true at once, and the V may simply be the shape where the two demands agree. But it does mean the flock is doing arithmetic. The bird at the point of the V is paying for the birds behind it, which is why the point keeps changing, and why a skein of geese in November is not really a line of birds. It is one long calculation, worked out in muscle, about how to spend less.
